heading: Health Inequalities Team
intro: The Health Inequalities Team (HIT) is based in the Population Health Sciences Institute at Newcastle University.

inequalitiesSection.heading: What are health inequalities?
inequalitiesSection.definition: Health inequalities are systematic, unfair and avoidable differences in health between groups of people. They can be seen in how long people live, the conditions they experience, and their access to, experience of and outcomes from health and care.

subsections.heading: Social determinants of health
subsections.body: Health is shaped by the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, together with their access to power, money and resources. Housing, education, employment, income and the local environment therefore influence opportunities for good health.

subsections.heading: The social gradient
subsections.body: Health does not divide neatly into a healthy advantaged group and an unhealthy disadvantaged group. Across society, health generally improves as social and economic position improves. This pattern is known as the social gradient in health.

aboutBody:
The Health Inequalities Team is based in the Population Health Sciences Institute at Newcastle University. We research why health outcomes differ so sharply between places and social groups, and what policy can do to close those gaps, across the social, economic, and political determinants of health.

We are an interdisciplinary team of social scientists, epidemiologists, geographers, economists, anthropologists, and clinical researchers. We use our range of expertise and a variety of methodological approaches to understand and explore health and care inequalities.

Among many national and international collaborators, we most closely work with the Newcastle PSRC, NENC ARC, and Health Equity North, to champion health inequalities research in the North of England.

The team is led by Clare Bambra, Professor of Public Health. Clare is a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, a member of the German National Academy of Sciences (Leopoldina), an NIHR Senior Investigator, and a founding co-Director of Health Equity North.
projectDescription:
There are four main workstreams in HIT.

Within these workstreams, there are multiple studies on a variety of topics spanning the intersection of health and inequalities.
